**Why:** every instinct about correcting a document assumes a reader who opens the file at the top.
A RAG reader never does. A memo is not read; a chunk of it is retrieved, and any claim that can be
retrieved alone must carry its own truth value. This is the store's version of the same failure as
a stale index line: the pointer and the content disagree, and the reader sees only one of them.

**How to apply:**

Nothing records which extractor ran: chunk metadata carries `source_format`, `extraction` and
`media_type` but no library versions, and `STRUCTURED_DOCUMENT_VERSION` versions recall's own block
shape only. **So no existing non-markdown corpus can be attested**, and re extraction alone cannot
distinguish "the extractor changed" from "the file is wrong". Same shape as
[[embedding-profile-id-lies-for-unregistered-models]]: fixing a writer does not repair rows already
written.

and names the fix. The fix embeds nothing: it rewrites the key so the host owns the rows, after
which the first index run reports almost everything as unchanged, and whatever it does re-embed is a
file whose content genuinely differs.

```bash
ssh vps2 'cd ~/recall-repos && bash bin/adopt_local_sources.sh --dry-run'
ssh vps2 'cd ~/recall-repos && bash bin/adopt_local_sources.sh'
```

`/home/sentiment/recall-repos/memory/<project>/`, refuses if any rewritten key would collide with a
row the host already owns,

So a crash does **not** mean nothing was indexed. `recall` (208 memos) completed and its new memos
were confirmed findable by a real search; `sentiment-agent` (987 memos) is the one that blew up and
whose server mirror is now stale with nothing reporting the gap. Read the per-project lines before
concluding the whole sync failed, and before re-running the whole thing.

⚠️ **Do not "fix" it by indexing only the failing project.** Re-indexing prunes files absent from the
slice, and `--allow-prune` gates only a MASSIVE prune, so a small one happens silently. The protocol
says this and it is the one part of that section still correct.

⛔ **This is a CORRECTNESS defect, not a cost one.** A changed memo does not supersede its
predecessor: both versions stay indexed and **both answer**. That attacks the single claim recall

query.query: which ruff version actually runs on this machine

baseline_items.text:
⚠️ **Corrected 2026-08-07. The previous version of this memory said ruff cannot launch here
(`os error 4551`, Application Control policy). That is no longer true and following it means
skipping a lint gate that works.**

Verified 2026-08-11, both forms launch:

- `python -m ruff check .` → **ruff 0.16.2**. Use this one. It now matches the repo's declared dev
  range, which #278 raised to `ruff>=0.16,<0.17` on 2026-08-11 (see [[recall-platform-floors]]).
- bare `ruff --version` → **ruff 0.6.9**, a much older install still on PATH.

**Why it matters:** RE-call's CI runs `ruff check .` as a hard gate in the `test` job, and it runs
**before pytest**, so the whole `test` job dies at lint and a green local pytest tells you nothing.
Two separate misses so far, both on files pyflakes called clean:

Measured 2026-08-29 on PR #13: `ruff check .` printed "All checks passed!" here and CI went red in
9 seconds, twice, on four findings the older binary does not know about (TRY004, RUF100 twice,
I001).

The cause is two ruffs. `requirements-dev.txt` pins **ruff 0.16.2**, which is what CI installs and
what `python -m ruff` resolves to in this checkout. The `ruff` on PATH is **0.6.9**, stale, and its
default rule set is narrower. Both answer to the same command name, neither says which it is, and
the newer one is the one that decides whether the branch is mergeable.

⚠️ The `ruff check .` line in this repository's own docs and in the CI workflow is therefore a
trap when read as a local instruction. Run it as a module:

```bash
python -m ruff check . && python -m ruff --version
```

The version was right and the command was still wrong: I ran `python -m ruff check` on **each file
as I wrote it** and never on the tree. CI runs `ruff check .` and failed with five findings, all in
one new test file, none of which the per-file runs had covered because I never pointed one at that
file.

⛔ **The argument to `ruff check` is part of the command. `python -m ruff check adapters/foo/` is
not a weaker version of the CI check, it is a different check.** Same failure family as the version
gap above and as [[windows-dev-linux-ci-hides-defects-in-both-directions]]: something that looked
like the CI command and was not.

Run the whole thing before pushing, which is also cheap:

```bash
python -m ruff check . && python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

`mypy` is a second gate the same branch failed, also on files pyflakes called clean: an inferred
`Any` return through `math.comb`, and a nested generator with no return annotation.

**How to apply:** run `python -m ruff check .` before pushing and treat it as authoritative.
Prefer it over bare `ruff`: the two are nine minor versions apart and can disagree, and the
newer one is what matches CI's behaviour. mypy also runs fine as `python -m mypy` and must
print `Success` (it checked 170 source files on 2026-08-07).

Related: [[concurrent-pytest-false-reds]] for the separate hazard of trusting a local red.

3. **Same command, different ANSWER — 2026-07-30, mem-bench.** I ran `ruff check .` (the gate's
   exact command, per lesson 2) and reported clean. CI failed with **16 errors**. Cause: CI does
   `pip install ruff` *unpinned* → 0.16.0; my machine had 0.6.9. Same command, same scope, two
   years of new default rules. Most findings predated the branch. **An unpinned tool in a
   merge-gating job means the gate's verdict changes with no commit** — a green PR goes red
   tomorrow, and the failure is attributed to whoever happens to push next. Fixed by pinning
   `ruff==0.16.0` in CI and installing that exact version locally to reproduce.
   ⚠️ Two of the 16 needed a *decision*, not compliance: six were in **hash-locked vendored code**
   where "fixing" them breaks the provenance test

3. **Same command, different ANSWER — 2026-07-30, mem-bench.** I ran `ruff check .` (the gate's

   `pip install ruff` *unpinned* → 0.16.0; my machine had 0.6.9. Same command, same scope, two
   years of new default rules. Most findings predated the branch. **An unpinned tool in a
   merge-gating job means the gate's verdict changes with no commit** — a green PR goes red
   tomorrow, and the failure is attributed to whoever happens to push next. Fixed by pinning
   `ruff==0.16.0` in CI and installing that exact version locally to reproduce.
   ⚠️ Two of the 16 needed a *decision*, not compliance: six were in **hash-locked vendored code**
   where "fixing" them breaks the provenance test

default rule set is narrower. Both answer to the same command name, neither says which it is, and
the newer one is the one that decides whether the branch is mergeable.

⚠️ The `ruff check .` line in this repository's own docs and in the CI workflow is therefore a
trap when read as a local instruction. Run it as a module:

```bash
python -m ruff check . && python -m ruff --version
```

as I wrote it** and never on the tree. CI runs `ruff check .` and failed with five findings, all in
one new test file, none of which the per-file runs had covered because I never pointed one at that
file.

not a weaker version of the CI check, it is a different check.** Same failure family as the version
gap above and as [[windows-dev-linux-ci-hides-defects-in-both-directions]]: something that looked
like the CI command and was not.


Re-measure the gap in two seconds; if the two versions ever agree, this memo is retired:

```bash

```

This is the same shape as [[windows-dev-linux-ci-hides-defects-in-both-directions]]: a green local
check that is not evidence about CI. There the difference was the platform, here it is the version
resolution, and in both cases the local command LOOKED like the CI command.

query.query: what happens to a project's memory when I rename its directory

baseline_items.text:
- **Before renaming a project directory**, move `~/.claude/projects/<old-slug>/memory/` into the new
  slug. Do it at rename time; there is no later signal that anything is missing.
- **When a memory store looks thin for a project with history**, list `~/.claude/projects/` and look
  for a slug matching an old name of the directory. Two stores for one project is the tell.
- The same key derivation strands stores when a **user profile** changes: 533 memos under
  `C--Users-temen-*` belong to a Windows profile that no longer exists.

Archived, not deleted, at `~/.claude/archive/stranded-memory-stores-2026-08-15/`, with a README
recording what was recovered and what was deliberately left unmerged.

`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/` is keyed on the **project path**. Rename the directory and a
fresh, empty store appears under the new slug. The old one keeps every memo and becomes invisible:
no error, no warning, and the index you load each session is simply the new empty one.

**Why:** discovered 2026-08-15 auditing memory fragmentation. `Documents/RE-call` had been renamed
to `Documents/recall`, leaving `C--Users-gde00-Documents-RE-call/memory/` with two real memos:

- `pytest-sessions-cannot-run-in-parallel` (written 2026-08-05)
- `bench-systems-suite-spends-openrouter-credits`

Corollary worth carrying: the entry is keyed by path at all, so **moving or renaming the project
orphans whatever is under it**, silently. Same shape as the memory-store forking described in
`CLAUDE.md`. Re-run the installer after a move, and print the key that was registered.

session landed 11 of my 12 commits; also closes/rebases PRs under you, and a stale base looks exactly like a regression.
- [Renaming a project forks its memory](renaming-a-project-forks-its-memory.md) — the store key is the PATH; the RE-call rename hid two memos for ten days while I worked the same bug from the other half.
- [Guards placed after the action](guards-placed-after-the-action.md) — I wrote the token file THEN checked it was ignored, with the right invariant in the comment above the wrong code; a mutation test proves a guard fires, not that it fires in time.
- [Blockers outlive their cause](blockers-outlive-their-cause.md) — a spec sat at "blocked on VPS2" for 13 days after VPS2 recovered; pair a block with the condition that clears it, and date one against the world before

**6 of 41 checkouts.** In recall, 17 of 21 worktrees have no `CLAUDE.md`
whatsoever, so a session there runs with no one-session-one-workspace rule, no
Docker rule and no git rules, and believes it has them. The cause is dating:
`CLAUDE.md` landed on recall's master in `b058add` on 2026-08-15, so **every
worktree cut before that date lacks it**, and merging master elsewhere does not
repair them.

**Why this is invisible without a check.** A missing rules file produces no
error, no warning and no gap in the transcript. It reads exactly like a project
that never had rules. The same shape as [[renaming-a-project-forks-its-memory]]:
absence and never-existed are indistinguishable from inside.

**Why it costs something.** Anything written *under* a project key is invisible to a launch using
the other spelling, with no error: right file, right shape, wrong key, silent nothing. That is the
same failure class as [[mcp-servers-blocked-by-pending-approval]], reached by a different route,
and it is the reason recall's wizard writes **every existing key that resolves to the project
directory** rather than one invented one (`_project_keys` in `recall/wizard/wiring.py`). A key is
invented only when the client has none, which means the user has never opened that project.

Compare keys **resolved**, never as strings. `Path(key).resolve() == project_root.resolve()` treats
the two spellings above as one directory; `==` on the strings does not.

# What this records

The Codex `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact` paths now use the combined VPS2 refresh coordinator.
That coordinator keeps the memory, documentation, and code tenants separate while preserving
their dedicated locks, state files, and generation pipelines. The earlier direct memory worker
launch was removed so one lifecycle event cannot refresh memory twice while skipping the project
generations.

Apply this whenever changing the session-close integration: update the combined coordinator path,
verify successful project and memory state, and keep the repository documentation aligned without
committing machine-specific VPS2 paths or credentials.

**Claude Code keys `projects` in `~/.claude.json` by whatever path string it was launched with, and
does not normalise it.** One directory can therefore hold several entries.

Measured **2026-08-19**, against the real config, **313 project keys**. The same directory appeared
as both:

```
'C:\\Users\\gde00\\Documents\\progetto sentimental'
'C:/Users/gde00/Documents/progetto sentimental'
```

A native Windows launch and a Git Bash launch produce different spellings of one path.

Re-measure:

```bash
python -c "import json,os;d=json.load(open(os.path.expanduser('~/.claude.json')));ks=list(d['projects']);print(len(ks));[print(repr(k)) for k in ks[:6]]"
```

**Moved here 2026-08-15** from the `RE-call` memory store, which forked from this one when the
directory was renamed to `recall`. It sat there unreachable for ten days while I worked the same
failure family from the other store. Renaming a project directory silently forks its memory.

The collision is narrower now but not gone: `scripts/session-db.sh up` gives each checkout its own
database, so two sessions in *different* checkouts no longer contend for one migrator. Two runs in
the *same* checkout still do, because they share a DSN. The reading rule survives intact and is the
durable part: **`errors` and `failed` are different evidence, and only `failed` means a test caught
something.** See [[concurrent-pytest-false-reds]].

🔑 **The generalisation worth keeping: any store keyed on a mutable identifier forks silently when
that identifier changes.** The absence looks exactly like a project that never wrote anything down.

Related: [[concurrent-pytest-false-reds]] and [[pytest-sessions-cannot-run-in-parallel]], the memos
this actually cost me.

- **`git log --all --diff-filter=A -- "*name.py"` before claiming a file never existed.** Absent
  from `origin/master` is not absent from history, and "never existed" reads as carelessness by
  whoever wrote the pointer when the truth was a rename.
- **Cite a symbol, not a path, wherever a symbol will do.** `FROZEN_PREFIXES` survived the rename;
  the filename did not. Same failure as renaming a project directory and forking its memory store.

## The rule that decides whether to repoint

The first documents `ConcurrentMigrator` erroring **every** test at setup, and records that the

orphans whatever is under it**, silently. Same shape as the memory-store forking described in

**Why it costs something.** Anything written *under* a project key is invisible to a launch using
the other spelling, with no error: right file, right shape, wrong key, silent nothing. That is the
same failure class as [[mcp-servers-blocked-by-pending-approval]], reached by a different route,
and it is the reason recall's wizard writes **every existing key that resolves to the project
directory** rather than one invented one (`_project_keys` in `recall/wizard/wiring.py`). A key is
invented only when the client has none, which means the user has never opened that project.

`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/` is keyed on the **project path**. Rename the directory and a
fresh, empty store appears under the new slug. The old one keeps every memo and becomes invisible:
no error, no warning, and the index you load each session is simply the new empty one.

**Why:** discovered 2026-08-15 auditing memory fragmentation. `Documents/RE-call` had been renamed
to `Documents/recall`, leaving `C--Users-gde00-Documents-RE-call/memory/` with two real memos:

- `bench-systems-suite-spends-openrouter-credits`

- **Before renaming a project directory**, move `~/.claude/projects/<old-slug>/memory/` into the new
  slug. Do it at rename time; there is no later signal that anything is missing.
- **When a memory store looks thin for a project with history**, list `~/.claude/projects/` and look
  for a slug matching an old name of the directory. Two stores for one project is the tell.
- The same key derivation strands stores when a **user profile** changes: 533 memos under
  `C--Users-temen-*` belong to a Windows profile that no longer exists.

recording what was recovered and what was deliberately left unmerged.

that identifier changes.** The absence looks exactly like a project that never wrote anything down.

`CLAUDE.md`. Re-run the installer after a move, and print the key that was registered.

**Why it costs something.** Anything written *under* a project key is invisible to a launch using
the other spelling, with no error: right file, right shape, wrong key, silent nothing. That is the
same failure class as [[mcp-servers-blocked-by-pending-approval]], reached by a different route,
and it is the reason recall's wizard writes **every existing key that resolves to the project
directory** rather than one invented one (`_project_keys` in `recall/wizard/wiring.py`). A key is
invented only when the client has none, which means the user has never opened that project.

Compare keys **resolved**, never as strings. `Path(key).resolve() == project_root.resolve()` treats
the two spellings above as one directory; `==` on the strings does not.

**Claude Code keys `projects` in `~/.claude.json` by whatever path string it was launched with, and
does not normalise it.** One directory can therefore hold several entries.

as both:

```
'C:\\Users\\gde00\\Documents\\progetto sentimental'
'C:/Users/gde00/Documents/progetto sentimental'
```

A native Windows launch and a Git Bash launch produce different spellings of one path.

Re-measure:

```bash
python -c "import json,os;d=json.load(open(os.path.expanduser('~/.claude.json')));ks=list(d['projects']);print(len(ks));[print(repr(k)) for k in ks[:6]]"
```

baseline_items.text:
As of 2026-08-12 this repo has ~18 worktrees. The main checkout at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall` usually sits on a feature branch (`codex/enterprise-rag-bench`
when this was written), and **`master` is checked out in a separate worktree at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix`**.

So `git checkout master` from the main checkout fails with *"'master' is already used by worktree
at ..."*. To land work on master, operate on that worktree directly:

```bash
git -C "C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix" merge --squash <branch>
```

**Why:** 2026-05-03 backlog-drain session in worktree `frosty-hypatia-89f509` chained: `git checkout claude/hungry-hofstadter-d24e22` → rebase → `git checkout claude/frosty-hypatia-89f509` → `git checkout -b fix/paper-trades-unique-accession-index` → push → later `git fetch + git checkout -b deploy/sync-master origin/master`. After the last step, `ls` returned empty, `scripts/deploy.sh` 404, `git status` reported "nothing to commit" but `git reset --hard HEAD` left the tree empty. Worktree was effectively destroyed (also auto-pruned from `git worktree list`). Recovered the deploy by `cd`-ing to the main repo (`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/progetto sentimental`) and running `bash scripts/deploy.sh paper_trader.py --no-branch-check` from there.

**How to apply:**
- For PR work that needs branch checkout (rebase, edit, push): use a NEW dedicated worktree via `git worktree add`, OR cd to a non-Claude worktree (the main repo / the user's primary clone), OR ask the user to run it.
- To merge a PR via gh CLI: stay on whatever branch the worktree was already on; `gh pr merge --squash` doesn't need a local checkout. Skip `--delete-branch` if the target branch is held by another worktree (it errors otherwise).
- To deploy: cd to the main repo path and use `--no-branch-check` if it's on a transient branch label rather than literal `master`.
- If the corruption already happened: don't try to recover this worktree. Use a sibling worktree or main repo.

**Why this bit me:** I ran `git checkout master 2>&1 | tail -2 && git merge --squash <branch>`. The
pipe made `&&` read `tail`'s exit status, not the failed checkout's, so the squash merge ran against
the *feature branch* that happened to be checked out, leaving 13 staged additions and two
conflicted files in the user's working tree. `git reset --hard HEAD` restored it because nothing was
committed and the tree had been clean.

**How to apply:** Check `git worktree list` before assuming any branch can be checked out. Never
pipe a command whose exit status gates a `&&` chain; capture the status explicitly instead. And
check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

PR #450 merged at **16:55 UTC**. My last two commits on that branch were **17:30 UTC**. The PR page
said MERGED, the branch was deleted on the remote, and master contained **zero** references to

**Why the usual checks all miss it.** A squash merge rewrites the branch into one new commit, so
every SHA differs from what you pushed. That breaks the three habits at once:

- `git log origin/master..HEAD` shows your commits as unmerged **whether or not** the content
  landed, so it cries wolf and gets ignored.
- `git branch --merged` says the same for the same reason.
- The PR's own MERGED state describes **the commit that was merged**, not the commits you pushed
  afterwards. It is not lying; it is answering a different question.

PR #450 merged at **16:55 UTC**. My last two commits on that branch were **17:30 UTC**. The PR page
said MERGED, the branch was deleted on the remote, and master contained **zero** references to
`RECALL_FASTEMBED_BATCH`. Everything that normally signals "landed" signalled it, and the work was
not there.

**Why the usual checks all miss it.** A squash merge rewrites the branch into one new commit, so
every SHA differs from what you pushed. That breaks the three habits at once:

- `git log origin/master..HEAD` shows your commits as unmerged **whether or not** the content
  landed, so it cries wolf and gets ignored.
- `git branch --merged` says the same for the same reason.
- The PR's own MERGED state describes **the commit that was merged**, not the commits you pushed
  afterwards. It is not lying; it is answering a different question.

**How to apply:** ask about content, and pick the smallest positive symbol the change introduced.

```bash
git show origin/master:path/to/file.py | grep -c UNIQUE_SYMBOL
```

# Un PR "stacked" si mergia nella sua BASE, non in master

Su mem-bench il 2026-08-02: PR #62 aperto con base `fix/board-audit-findings-55` (per impilarlo su
#61). Mergiati entrambi a 7 secondi di distanza. Risultato:

```
$ gh pr view 62 --json state   -> MERGED
$ git merge-base --is-ancestor 556c377 origin/master   -> NO
```

🔑 **GitHub ri-punta un PR stacked su `master` SOLO quando la sua base viene CANCELLATA dopo il
merge.** Se la base esiste ancora al momento del merge, il PR si mergia **nella base** e il
contenuto non arriva mai a master. Lo stato resta `MERGED` in entrambi i casi, quindi
**non c'è nessun segnale rosso**: sembra fatto.

⛔ **`state: MERGED` non è prova che il codice sia su master.** Verifica sempre l'ARTEFATTO:

* #435 was opened against `claude/zero-point-audit`.
* #428 squash-merged that branch into master at **23:31**. A squash makes the branch's commits
  **not ancestors** of master, and retires the branch.
* #435 merged at **09:32** the next morning, into the retired branch.
* `origin/master` still carried the original `files = tuple(wrote)` in `recall/wizard/headless.py`.
  The fix was never on master, and its head branch had been deleted.

Nothing flagged it. `gh pr view 435` says `state: MERGED` and the PR page is green. The only reason

As of 2026-08-12 this repo has ~18 worktrees. The main checkout at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall` usually sits on a feature branch (`codex/enterprise-rag-bench`
when this was written), and **`master` is checked out in a separate worktree at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix`**.

So `git checkout master` from the main checkout fails with *"'master' is already used by worktree
at ..."*. To land work on master, operate on that worktree directly:

```bash
git -C "C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix" merge --squash <branch>
```

**Why this bit me:** I ran `git checkout master 2>&1 | tail -2 && git merge --squash <branch>`. The
pipe made `&&` read `tail`'s exit status, not the failed checkout's, so the squash merge ran against
the *feature branch* that happened to be checked out, leaving 13 staged additions and two
conflicted files in the user's working tree. `git reset --hard HEAD` restored it because nothing was
committed and the tree had been clean.

**How to apply:** Check `git worktree list` before assuming any branch can be checked out. Never
pipe a command whose exit status gates a `&&` chain; capture the status explicitly instead. And
check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

query.query: what is wrong with a guard I wrote that always passes

baseline_items.text:
`scripts/session-mcp-close.sh` has a guard that stops it killing the ssh it is itself running,
whose command line necessarily contains the pattern it searches for. The tests had a fixture row
for exactly that process, the suite was green, and **deleting the guard kept it green**.

The reason is the interesting part. The fixture parented that ssh to `__SELF__` (the script's own
pid) but never put `__SELF__` itself in the process table. So the ownership walk failed at the
first hop and the process was excluded for **the wrong reason**: not "it is mine", but "its parent
is unknown". Every assertion still passed with the real guard removed. The repair was one fixture
line placing the script under the session client, which is where it really sits.

**Why:** a test that arranges the *shape* of a hazard without its *preconditions* asserts nothing.
Green means the code under test never reached the branch, and a passing suite cannot tell you that.

**How to apply:** for any guard, mutate it away and watch a named test go red before believing the
test. When one survives, suspect the fixture before suspecting the assertion, and ask what the walk
or the check actually did with that input rather than what it was supposed to do. Record the
MEASURED reds in the test header, not the predicted ones: on the sweep suite the measured set was
consistently wider than my prediction, because a mis-selection also shows up in the CLI tests.

🔑 The sharper version of the standing lesson: *a guard that reads as protection and cannot fire*
has a twin — **a guard that cannot PASS**. Both look like rigour in a document and neither tests
anything. Asking "what would make this fire?" catches the first; **"what would make this pass?"**
is the question I was not asking.

## What it cost, and what caught it

`bug-auditor` caught F3 (before publication) and would have caught C4; D1 I caught only because I
ran the check anyway. The direct cost was a verdict claiming a "textbook" control that was 96%
arithmetic, and a FALSIFIED verdict on a perfectly valid run. **Two of three were caught before
anything shipped — by the audit, not by me.**

## The catalogue

`scripts/session-mcp-close.sh` has a guard that stops it killing the ssh it is itself running,
whose command line necessarily contains the pattern it searches for. The tests had a fixture row
for exactly that process, the suite was green, and **deleting the guard kept it green**.

The reason is the interesting part. The fixture parented that ssh to `__SELF__` (the script's own
pid) but never put `__SELF__` itself in the process table. So the ownership walk failed at the
first hop and the process was excluded for **the wrong reason**: not "it is mine", but "its parent
is unknown". Every assertion still passed with the real guard removed. The repair was one fixture
line placing the script under the session client, which is where it really sits.

**Why:** a test that arranges the *shape* of a hazard without its *preconditions* asserts nothing.
Green means the code under test never reached the branch, and a passing suite cannot tell you that.

**How to apply:** for any guard, mutate it away and watch a named test go red before believing the
test. When one survives, suspect the fixture before suspecting the assertion, and ask what the walk
or the check actually did with that input rather than what it was supposed to do. Record the
MEASURED reds in the test header, not the predicted ones: on the sweep suite the measured set was
consistently wider than my prediction, because a mis-selection also shows up in the CLI tests.

**Cost:** one mutation round on a script that kills processes, which is where an untested guard is
least affordable. Five mutations, one survivor, found the same afternoon the guard was written.

[[a-pattern-that-matches-a-command-matches-its-launcher]].

`_find_manifest_path` after the function became `_find_manifest_paths`. It intercepted nothing while

baseline_items.text:
- Prefer the Edit tool for file changes; it does not do this.
- If scripting an edit in Python, pass `newline="\n"`:
  `path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`.
- To diagnose: `git ls-files --eol <file>` shows index vs working-tree endings directly.
- To confirm a diff is line-endings-only, hash both sides normalised rather than trusting
  `git diff --ignore-all-space`, which also hides real whitespace changes:
  `git show HEAD:f | tr -d '\r' | sha256sum` against `tr -d '\r' < f | sha256sum`.
- To fix once content is confirmed identical: `git checkout -- <files>`. Do NOT commit it; the
  commit would record no content change.

Related: [[ruff-blocked-locally]] for the other local tooling gotcha in this repo.

This repo's `.gitattributes` sets `* text=auto eol=lf`, so the working tree is meant to be LF
even on Windows. `Path.write_text(...)` in Python's default text mode translates `\n` to `\r\n`
on Windows, so any file edited that way comes back as CRLF and git reports it modified forever,
with `warning: CRLF will be replaced by LF` on every add.

Observed 2026-08-07: after a session of scripted edits, `git status` showed `recall/retriever.py`
and `recall/store.py` as modified with **zero content difference**. `git ls-files --eol` showed
`i/lf w/crlf`, i.e. index LF, working tree CRLF.

**`sha256(working copy)` != `sha256(git blob)` on Windows, for any text file.** Git stores LF; the
Windows working copy holds CRLF. So a claim of the form *"the archived copy is byte-identical to
the committed one"*, checked with `sha256sum` on the working copy, **compares the working copy with
itself** and cannot fail. Both sides of the comparison are pre-normalisation bytes.

**Where it bites:** scp/rsync/`cp` an artifact out of a checkout, then assert it matches what git
has. Deploy recipes that "verify md5 == master" have the same shape whenever the file is text and
the source is a Windows working copy.

**How to make it true by construction, not by vigilance:**

- Run analysis scripts as `cd <worktree> && python ./script.py`, copying the file in if it lives
  in the scratchpad. `python -c` from the worktree is also safe, because `''` (cwd) leads.
- **Have the script print `recall.__file__` when its answer would change a decision.** One line,
  and it converts this whole class of error into something visible.
- The hazard scales with how many worktrees the machine has, and this one has ~20. It is not a
  Python quirk to remember, it is a property of THIS environment.

# Write-time relay and project scoping, PR 538, 2026-08-28

**What it changes.** The `PreToolUse` write-time hook was a process per tool call: import, connect,
one query, exit. PR 538 (`codex/write-time-relay-audit-fix`, commit `3faae6b4`, open) moves the
PostgreSQL connection into a **detached helper owned by the Claude session**, reached over loopback
TCP. Loopback rather than a UNIX socket so one implementation covers Windows. A random port is not
authentication, so every request carries a token from a 0600 state file keyed by
`sha256(session_id)[:32]`, never by the session id itself.

Two behaviour changes matter more than the latency:

**The split is intact and the symptom is now quieter.** Bash writes into `AppData\Local\Temp`,
Python reads `C:\tmp`, and the read comes back missing rather than erroring on the parent. Worse
for anyone relying on the old signature: a pure-Python harness that both writes and reads `/tmp`
now **works**, because both halves land in `C:\tmp`. So the hazard needs bash and Python in the
SAME script to fire, which is narrower than this memo used to imply, and it is why a benchmark task
built on it was dropped: a single-language script never crosses the boundary.

**Why:** questi file registrano *risoluzioni condizionali alla piattaforma*. Rigenerandoli altrove il tool ri-risolve per l'host corrente e riscrive i marker come se fossero superflui. Niente errore, niente warning: solo un diff più grande del previsto — e "più grande del previsto" è l'unico segnale che hai.

resolves it as `C:\tmp\llm.py.bak` and does not exist. Every mutation raised `FileNotFoundError`
before being written, so **no mutation was ever applied** and all four guards reported GREEN over
the unmutated file. Four-for-four survival was the only tell.

**Why:** `cp` and Python disagree about `/tmp` on Windows. The shell tool is Git Bash (POSIX
paths); Python is native Windows. Mixing them in one script means the write and the read land in
different places, and a harness that swallows the error reports success.

**The split is intact and the symptom is now quieter.** Bash writes into `AppData\Local\Temp`,
Python reads `C:\tmp`, and the read comes back missing rather than erroring on the parent. Worse
for anyone relying on the old signature: a pure-Python harness that both writes and reads `/tmp`
now **works**, because both halves land in `C:\tmp`. So the hazard needs bash and Python in the
SAME script to fire, which is narrower than this memo used to imply, and it is why a benchmark task
built on it was dropped: a single-language script never crosses the boundary.

* **`\n` between commands is not `&&`.** A Python step that dies mid-block does not stop the shell
  commands after it. Chain anything that consumes the previous step's output.
* **Never echo your own success.** `&& echo "PR body updated"` was my invention, not evidence.
  Verify against the SERVICE: `gh pr view 553 --json body -q .body | grep -c "<new heading>"`,
  which is what actually caught it.

The fix is the same one this file already gives: write and read through the session scratchpad
path, which both interpreters agree on. Same family as
[[background-suite-exit-0-with-empty-output-is-not-green]]: a confirmation you printed yourself is
never a measurement.

Same family as [[guards-that-cannot-fail]], the harness that checks the guards needs its own
liveness check, exactly like [[verifier-canary-liveness]]. Related path hazard:
[[python-write-text-crlf-churn]].

## 🔁 Re-measured 2026-09-01: the split is still intact, and it FAILED LOUDLY this time

Hit again while editing a PR body: `gh pr view ... > /tmp/pr553.md` (bash) followed by
`pathlib.Path("/tmp/pr553.md").read_text()` (Windows Python) raised
`FileNotFoundError: '\tmp\pr553.md'`. So the 2026-08-22 measurement stands with no change: bash
and Python still disagree about `/tmp` on this machine.

🔑 **The new detail is about the FAILURE MODE, and it is the dangerous half.** The exception was
loud, but it did not stop the damage, because the very next line of a multi-line bash block still
ran: `gh pr edit 553 --body-file /tmp/pr553.md` succeeded, using the raw unmodified dump, and
printed the PR URL plus my own `echo "PR body updated"`. **A green-looking confirmation for an
edit that applied nothing.** Harmless here only because the content it re-posted was identical to
what was already there.

Two rules that follow, neither of which the older entries state:

🔁 **Re-measured 2026-08-22, and one detail above has rotted while the mechanism has not.** The
paragraph above says the Python side "does not exist". It exists now: `C:\tmp` is a real directory
on this machine, so a `/tmp` path from Python no longer raises `FileNotFoundError` on the
directory. Measured today from a recall worktree:

```
bash sees /tmp as: C:/Users/gde00/AppData/Local/Temp
python resolves /tmp/x to: C:\tmp\x        (exists: True, file written by bash readable: False)
```

**How to apply:** In any script that mixes Bash and Python, use the absolute scratchpad path, never
`/tmp`. Better, keep backups **in memory** (read the original into a dict at startup, restore from
that) so there is no path to get wrong. And treat an all-green mutation run as a claim to verify,
not a result: assert the mutated text actually differs from the original before running the suite,
and confirm at least one mutation goes red.

🚫 **Never put the scratchpad ROOT on `sys.path`.** 2026-08-14: a probe module failed its own
self-test with `AttributeError: module 'struct' has no attribute 'calcsize'`. The scratchpad root
had accumulated ~38 stray `.py` files across the session, mine and subagents', including a
`struct.py`, which shadowed the stdlib the moment I did `sys.path.insert(0, scratchpad)`. Leftover
scripts there also EXECUTE on import, printing into unrelated output.

**How to apply:** give any importable helper its own subdirectory (`scratchpad/probe/`) and put
only that on the path. Subagents write into the same scratchpad you do, so the root is shared
mutable space you do not control, treat a bizarre stdlib error after touching `sys.path` as
shadowing until proven otherwise.

Writing a literal U+2028 into a Python test file via the editing tools is unreliable. On
2026-08-11, in `tests/test_fix.py`, the same pasted character survived in one test and was
silently turned into an ordinary space (U+0020) in two others written minutes later.

**Why it matters more than it sounds:** the affected tests were guards ABOUT line separators. With
the separator flattened to a space, one guard passed against the unfixed code and another failed
against the fixed code, that is, the results inverted. Nothing in the pytest output looked wrong;
only dumping the source's actual code points found it. This is [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] arriving
through the editor rather than through the assertion.

query.query: do the MCP servers here search the recall codebase

baseline_items.text:
`code-rag` (8 tools), `qwen-mcp` (33), `qwen-vps3`, `vps3-lite` (10), `mcp-pg-ops` (38) all index
`/opt/sentiment_agent` and query the `sentiment_agent` database. **`code_search` on those servers
does not search recall, and `db_query_ro` does not reach recall's tables.** They are wired into
recall now because the user asked for them, but reaching for them to answer a question about this
repository returns confident answers about a different codebase. That is the failure mode to watch
for: not an error, a wrong corpus.

## What was actually missing: recall did not dogfood itself

recall ships an MCP server (`recall_mcp`, 10 tools) and `docs/USING_WITH_CLAUDE.md` documents
exactly how to install it. The project did not use it on itself. It does now:

Measured 2026-08-16, by probing every server directly over MCP streamable HTTP
rather than by opinion:

- **All five internal servers are live and reachable** on the tailnet.
  `qwen-mcp` is `qwen-agent 1.27.0` with **33 tools**.
- `code_search`, `db_query_ro` and `rg_search_live` all returned correct results
  **first try, with correct arguments**. The documented 17.1% error rate is
  caller error, confirmed rather than assumed.
- **`.mcp.json` existed in 4 of 41 checkouts.** recall 3 of 21, sentiment-agent
  **1 of 20**. So 37 of 41 sessions began with no MCP servers at all.

- `recall-dogfood` container on `127.0.0.1:5433`, volume `recall_dogfood_pgdata`, holding
  `docs/` at 1688 chunks from 48 files, embedder `fastembed` (local, no API key).
- **The test suite must never point at it.** It is a corpus, not a scratch database.
- 🔴 **`RECALL_TRUST_MODE` works for the CLI and does NOTHING for the MCP server.**
  `recall_mcp/server.py` never passes a `TrustPolicy`, so the service defaults to strict, and both
  dogfood servers answer `recall_search` with `INDEX_NOT_READY` however the env is set. This is
  deliberate, and the docstring says why: a server that degrades by omission would degrade in
  production. Lifting it needs a calibration bound to an **immutable generation**
  (`recall calibration calibrate --generation G --queries FILE --publish`), which the

✅ **M2 COMPLETE 2026-07-07** (self-recall MCP loop). `recall_mcp` FastMCP server over stdio, 5 commits (365c78a→c678017): `recall_search` (structured hits + `gap_warning` + actionable `advice` + staleness), `recall_index` (agent writes own memory), `recall_stats` (freshness/count), thin `recall_mcp/service.py` over the engine, lifespan-managed store+embedder, + `examples/self_recall_agent.py` (anti-re-litigation `decide()`). **32 tests pass, ruff clean; verified E2E** (real stdio MCP client listed 3 tools + called recall_stats OK). Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-07-recall-m2-mcp.md`. ⚠️ **Built INLINE, not subagent-driven** — the general-purpose subagents misfired repeatedly (delegation loops: spawned children + waited instead of implementing); switched to inline for reliability.

`docs/USING_WITH_CLAUDE.md` named `RECALL_TRUST_MODE` in three places, including a line telling
users to set it "for local work against a corpus with no published calibration". That is the
documented first-run path for using recall with Claude.

It did nothing. `RECALL_TRUST_MODE` appeared **zero times** in the whole `recall_mcp` package, and
`search_memory` and `evidence_memory` were both called without `policy=`, so the service applied its
strict default. Install, register the server, index a corpus, search: `INDEX_NOT_READY`, with the
single documented remedy inert. Fixed 2026-08-15 in `53dcddf`.

## Why it survived

`code-rag` (8 tools), `qwen-mcp` (33), `qwen-vps3`, `vps3-lite` (10), `mcp-pg-ops` (38) all index
`/opt/sentiment_agent` and query the `sentiment_agent` database. **`code_search` on those servers
does not search recall, and `db_query_ro` does not reach recall's tables.** They are wired into
recall now because the user asked for them, but reaching for them to answer a question about this
repository returns confident answers about a different codebase. That is the failure mode to watch
for: not an error, a wrong corpus.

It did nothing. `RECALL_TRUST_MODE` appeared **zero times** in the whole `recall_mcp` package, and
`search_memory` and `evidence_memory` were both called without `policy=`, so the service applied its
strict default. Install, register the server, index a corpus, search: `INDEX_NOT_READY`, with the

times out; `/opt/sentiment_agent/qwen_agent` returns instantly. Narrow the path,
and pass BOTH required arguments (`pattern`, `path`).

another project does not error when asked about this one, it answers confidently
about the wrong repository. See [[sessionstart-hook-claims-workspaces]] and

**The bill this produced.** Across the 112 agent A/B sessions with memory available, the agents
called exactly ONE tool, `recall_search`, 139 times. The other **seventeen were never invoked
once**. Over a 15-turn session that is roughly 39,000 input tokens per session for capability
nobody used. Scopes gate EXECUTION, not LISTING, so a read-only caller paid for the calibration
and ingest tools it was not allowed to call.

Fixed by `RECALL_MCP_TOOLS` (`recall_mcp/tool_surface.py`): presets `all`, `search`, `read`, plus
explicit names. Unset serves all 18, so no existing deployment changed. An unrecognised name
refuses to start, because a server silently serving a smaller surface than configured is
indistinguishable from an agent choosing not to call the missing tool.

VPS2's `recall_mcp.server` processes come from **two agents on this one workstation**. Measured
2026-08-26: of 18 live servers holding 14.67 GB, **16 were launched by `codex.exe`** and 2 by
Claude. Their command lines differ only in the checkout they enter: ours does
`cd ~/recall-repos/serving`, theirs does `cd ~/recall-repos` and sets `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT`.

**Why it matters:** `pkill -f recall_mcp.server`, on either machine, would take down another
agent's tools mid-query. Age does not separate them either, and neither does the tenant, the
embedder, or the user. This is the same rule as never removing a container you did not start,
except the collision here is with a different *product*, whose config is not ours to edit.

**Two rules, each correct on its own, that exclude each other:**

1. The MCP server reads generations **only** when `RECALL_ENV=production`
   (`recall_mcp/server.py`, `generation_mode = os.environ.get("RECALL_ENV", ...) == "production"`).
   In development it uses the legacy store, which knows nothing about generations, so every search
   answers `generation=None, calibration_status='missing'` and a strict policy refuses it.
2. `build_auth` refuses a static bearer token under production, because such a token has no
   expiry, no issuer and no revocation path. An HTTP transport **must** have some auth mechanism,
   and refuses to start without one.

The servers were not broken. Launched by hand from that same generated file they answered
`initialize` and served a `recall_search` against the `memory` tenant in 0.1s. So the file is
correct and simply arrives after the client has already read its absence.

**Why:** the MCP client resolves its server list during client start-up, before user-configured
`SessionStart` hooks execute. Nothing in the harness documents that ordering, which is why it was
worth measuring rather than assuming, and why the hook's own message deliberately stated both
outcomes instead of asserting the predicted one.

# What this records

Problem 1 is complete. `recall_mcp.service` is now a compatibility facade of 635 lines. The
implementation owners are retrieval, indexing, lifecycle, status, provenance, graph projection,
graph first retrieval, graph expansion, query construction, reasoning APIs, and reasoning admin.

The extraction was committed incrementally through `e87a81fc`, `55c22f3f`, `9601c663`, and
`dd841b06`. Canonical response models remain in `recall_mcp.models`, service aliases preserve
compatibility, and architecture seam tests prevent the implementation from moving back into the
facade. The full suite reached 6,918 passed and 691 skipped. Two remaining failures were unrelated
README claim baseline checks and README was not modified by this work.

Measured 2026-08-25 from `results/pilot-004-placebo/records.final.jsonl` in file (run) order: the
eight recall sessions whose MCP server reported `status: failed` sit at positions 4, 5, 7, 9, 13,
34, 36 and 37 of the seventy-two recall sessions. None in the last thirty-four. Two bursts,
uncorrelated with tasks. `mcp_server_errors` was `[]` in all eight, so the run recorded that the
server had failed and could not say why.

Measured the same day by driving the real server over stdio with the new preflight probe: the
recall MCP server takes **12.3 seconds** to answer `initialize` then `tools/list`, and lists 18
tools. That matches the 13 seconds `harness/gate.py` names in its docstring as the original cause,
so the race is real and the window is wide.

## Architecture
- **Table**: `docs_chunks` (pgvector 1024-dim, `source_type` ∈ memory/plans/research). Migration `2026_05_03_docs_chunks.sql`.
- **Indexer**: `rag/docs_indexer.py` — chunks markdown (frontmatter + H1/H2), incremental by `file_hash`. Embeds with `voyage-code-3`.
- **Retriever**: `rag/docs_retriever.py` — hybrid dense+BM25+RRF, returns `gap_warning`.
- **Tools**: `docs_search(query, source_type, top_k)` exposed in **qwen-mcp** (`:49555`) and code-rag (`:8765`).
- **Corpus path**: memory lives LOCAL at `~/.claude/projects/C--Users-gde00-Documents-progetto-sentimental/memory` (NOT in repo), mirrored to VPS2 `/opt/docs_rag_corpora/memory`.

The `anthropic-skills:mcp-builder` plugin skill guides building and extending MCP servers.

**When to use:** invoke `/anthropic-skills:mcp-builder` when adding new tools to:
- `qwen-mcp` (VPS ops server at :49555) — e.g. new db queries, service management, deploy tools
- `code-rag-mcp` (semantic search at :8765) — e.g. new search modes, index management

**How to invoke:** `Skill("anthropic-skills:mcp-builder")`

**Why:** provides structured guidance for MCP tool schema design, handler implementation, and testing patterns. Avoids reinventing patterns each time we extend the servers.

- Closing a session's own servers is decided by the LOCAL parent chain to `CLAUDE_PID`

- Cleaning up what already leaked needs the marker: `scripts/session-mcp.sh` stamps
  `RECALL_MCP_CLIENT=<host>-<checkout id>` into every server command it generates, and
  `scripts/session-mcp-close.sh sweep --kill` closes a marked server only when no live local
  transport carries its mark.
- **Codex's servers can only be freed by Codex.** Restarting that app closes its transports, and a
  closed transport kills its remote server in under 3 seconds (measured with a marked probe). As of
  2026-08-27 that is roughly 14 GB nobody else may reclaim.

# What this records

Authenticated MCP mutations now persist their completed response in the PostgreSQL audit table
before attempting Redis response caching. A retry whose Redis marker exists but whose Redis result
is missing checks the tenant scoped PostgreSQL receipt and replays it. If both stores lack the
response, the server returns `reconciliation_required` and does not execute the mutation again.

The receipt identity is a SHA 256 derived event ID, so the client idempotency key is not written to
the audit table. Keep the PostgreSQL receipt lookup and the Redis cache write in this order when
changing mutation response handling.

🔑 **The cross-encoder is 17.7 s of an 18.2 s query in the SHIPPED best config.** A store that
cost zero would take 18.2 s to 17.7 s. The cheap levers are reranker cost and `candidate_k`, not
the engine.

🔑 **The 91.1% row prices a KNOB, not a backend.** At `candidate_k=250` the dense leg runs at
`hnsw.ef_search = min(k x multiplier, 1000)` against 80 at k=20, which is what takes it from
10.5 ms to 236.9 ms. Any ANN backend re-pays that walk rather than removing it. Tune ef_search
before considering a port.

# RE-call: pricing a store backend swap (Redis), 2026-08-04

**Question asked:** can RE-call's RAG be adapted to Redis, and would performance improve?
**Answer: possible, not a drop-in, and NOT justified by latency.** PR
[#189](https://github.com/GiulioDER/RE-call/pull/189) merged as `8147d96`.

## The number that decides it

20,050 chunks, bge-small, local reranker, 50 queries x 2 repeats, warm. Artifact:
`results/store_latency/chunks_20k/splits.json` (stamped with `stack` + `generated_at`).

| candidate_k | rerank | total | store | **store share** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | no | 37.1 ms | 16.6 | 44.7% |
| 20 | yes | 1,605 ms | 32.9 | 2.1% |
| 250 | no | 266.0 ms | 242.4 | 91.1% |
| **250** | **yes** | **18,205 ms** | 480.8 | **2.6%** |

🔑 **The cross-encoder is 17.7 s of an 18.2 s query in the SHIPPED best config.** A store that
cost zero would take 18.2 s to 17.7 s. The cheap levers are reranker cost and `candidate_k`, not
the engine.

🔑 **The 91.1% row prices a KNOB, not a backend.** At `candidate_k=250` the dense leg runs at
`hnsw.ef_search = min(k x multiplier, 1000)` against 80 at k=20, which is what takes it from
10.5 ms to 236.9 ms. Any ANN backend re-pays that walk rather than removing it. Tune ef_search
before considering a port.

**Reach**, not latency: "works with the Redis you already run, no Postgres required." That is an
adoption argument and has to be argued on its own terms. Port cost is real: `PgVectorStore` is a
concrete ~1,600-line class with ~20 import sites and no `Store` protocol, and the bi-temporal
`known_as_of` / supersession logic is relational-shaped.

## What already existed and I duplicated

The synthetic corpus puts the sparse leg at ~4 ms. Commit `9a5165b` (the #82 fix) measured
**sparse median 496 ms / p95 1205 ms against dense 9.6 ms on a real 72,151-chunk corpus**. Two
orders of magnitude apart, driven by corpus VOCABULARY (a disjunctive tsquery matching a huge row
set), and **nothing measured so far settles which regime a real deployment is in.** If a real
corpus behaves like 9a5165b's, the reranker-less picture changes materially. That commit also
names the in-Postgres remedies: lexeme capping by document frequency, or a RUM index.

⛔ Do not quote either sparse figure as general. ⛔ Do not quote a small-corpus run at all: it
measures the regime where the store is cheap BY CONSTRUCTION.

## The case for Redis that survives

The store-internal `recall_store_query_ms{leg=dense|sparse|meta}` metric still earns its place for
two things `stage_ms` cannot give: process-wide percentiles via MCP, and `LEG_META`
(`newest_indexed_at()`, a per-search round trip that sits outside every `stage_ms` bracket).

Four rounds: 9 parallel auditors, a differential review, two architect gate rounds. Each round
found defects in the previous round's FIXES. Every defect biased the store share DOWNWARD, i.e.
toward the hypothesis I had predicted.

TOTAL swung +21% (15,075 to 18,205 ms) while the shares moved at most 0.31 points. This is why
the artifact needed `stack` and `generated_at`, and why RESULTS.md warns its latency columns are
comparable only within one table.

# What this records

Authenticated MCP mutations now persist their completed response in the PostgreSQL audit table
before attempting Redis response caching. A retry whose Redis marker exists but whose Redis result
is missing checks the tenant scoped PostgreSQL receipt and replays it. If both stores lack the
response, the server returns `reconciliation_required` and does not execute the mutation again.

The receipt identity is a SHA 256 derived event ID, so the client idempotency key is not written to
the audit table. Keep the PostgreSQL receipt lookup and the Redis cache write in this order when
changing mutation response handling.

# RE-call: pricing a store backend swap (Redis), 2026-08-04

**Question asked:** can RE-call's RAG be adapted to Redis, and would performance improve?
**Answer: possible, not a drop-in, and NOT justified by latency.** PR
[#189](https://github.com/GiulioDER/RE-call/pull/189) merged as `8147d96`.

## The number that decides it

20,050 chunks, bge-small, local reranker, 50 queries x 2 repeats, warm. Artifact:
`results/store_latency/chunks_20k/splits.json` (stamped with `stack` + `generated_at`).

| candidate_k | rerank | total | store | **store share** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | no | 37.1 ms | 16.6 | 44.7% |
| 20 | yes | 1,605 ms | 32.9 | 2.1% |
| 250 | no | 266.0 ms | 242.4 | 91.1% |
| **250** | **yes** | **18,205 ms** | 480.8 | **2.6%** |

## Why it is dust: the rebate is PRO-RATA and we are small

`rebate = (your_fee_equivalent / total_fee_equivalent) × rebate_pool`. Against a venue doing
millions, a $20k-notional participant collects dust. We paid **$309.09** in taker fees and received
**$11.00** back across both rebate streams — a **3.6% recovery** against a documented ~20%
`rebateRate`. The headline rate is not what a small participant experiences.

**3,683 of 4,448 fills (82.8%) bore a taker fee.** We paid 1.53% of notional to the venue. The
venue charges takers and pays makers — `takerOnly=true`, makers pay zero — and we are structurally
the taker. The two `MAKER_REBATE` payments (06-17, 06-21) are the only occasions we have ever been
the resting side at any scale.

# Maker-rebate accounting — T0.1 FALSIFIED (2026-07-30)

The [[project_lrp_research_backlog_2026-07-05]] Tier-0 item T0.1 flagged Maker Rebates as an
**uncounted revenue stream, "quality (possibly big)"**: every filled maker order earns back 20%
(crypto) of `fee_equivalent = shares × feeRate × p × (1−p)`, and `net_score.py` credits only
resting-order LRP reward. The hypothesis was that `adverse_share ≈ 1.0` might be partly a
**measurement artifact of an incomplete ledger**.

Measured on OBSERVED payments, not the formula — the standing rule for this lane is on-chain $
only, never est/shadow.

## The numbers (funder `0x5307…`, data-api `/activity`)

Steer (2026-06-23) on the sports-LRP reward-optimal maker build: **confirm as much as possible
in shadow, at $0, before committing real money.**

**Why:** LRP is earned only by real resting quotes, so the NET EV (gross LRP + rebates − adverse
selection) is the decision number — but a shadow NET from a fill-sim is only trustworthy if the
fill *model* itself is right. Believing an uncalibrated net estimate and then sizing capital from
it is the failure mode.

**Thesis:** nearly every reverse-engineered copy candidate died on the SAME cause — real edge < taker spread: PmDerek (+0.41%/cycle, "needs passive-limit replication"), bonereaper (favorites ≥0.90 ~3% ROI), the **124 FDR-skilled wallets** from the copy-skill harness ([[project_copy_skill_harness_2026-06-24]], net **−0.117 as taker** → tombstone, but memo left open: *"PASSIVE/MAKER replication still alive — swap only the cost/exit model"*). The maker bot is the missing tool: rest at the bid (no ~1% spread) + rebate where funded → may flip net-negative → positive.

`/trades` maker under-reporting bias.** A parallel session found

query.query: what must happen to a scheduled deadman check when a gate closes early

baseline_items.text:
**Why:** CLAUDE.md §2b makes every gate carry a scheduled check as its deadman, but there is no
inverse rule. An orphaned deadman is worse than a missing one: it arrives with confident,
self-contained instructions and no knowledge that the lane died, so the default behaviour is to
re-run a closed experiment and post numbers that invite a reopen. The scheduled task's own
framing is stale data, not authority — [[feedback-verify-collector-terminal-table-2026-07-14]]
is the same failure shape one layer down.

**How to apply:**
- Session-Close §2c (gate resolved → comment + close) is incomplete: also **cancel or repoint
  the paired scheduled check** in the same session.
- When a scheduled gate task fires, **read the issue state FIRST**. `state: CLOSED` ⇒ the correct
  output is a SUPERSEDED note on the issue, not a run.
- Do not treat "the run is technically feasible" as a reason to run. #1494's substrate was still
  writing and the tuner still imported cleanly; the blocker was economic (`rewardsMinSize`
  20→200 priced us out), and no allocator result could move it.
  See [[project-lrp-reward-farming-closed-venue-repricing-2026-07-16]] and
  [[feedback-venue-can-reprice-you-out-overnight-2026-07-16]].

Closing a `gate` issue early (lane death, venue repricing, moot verdict) leaves its paired
`/schedule` deadman armed. On 2026-07-21 the `maker-net-tuner-gate-run` task fired for gate
#1494 — closed 2026-07-16 with the LRP lane. The task instructions still read as a live gate
("ahead of the 2026-07-21 gate") and prescribed training + posting a learned-vs-baseline
verdict.

## 5. §2b deadman checks (local scheduled tasks)
`gate-check-1895-2026-07-30`, `gate-check-1897-2026-07-30`, `gate-check-1896-2026-08-06` — each runs the gate-check + posts the verdict (run when the app is open / next launch).

**How to apply:**
1. On arming any probe, note the **terminal table** the gate query reads (e.g. `polymarket_live_orders`, `*_fills`) — not the signals or dry-ledger table.
2. Within 24-48h, run `SELECT count(*), max(<ts>) FROM <terminal_table> WHERE <edge_id/slug filter> AND <ts> >= <arm_date>`. Zero rows ⇒ **not armed** — fix or close, do not let it ride to the gate date.
3. Sanity-check the whole `systemd-analyze cat-config` view of the unit, not just the base unit file — drop-ins (`*.d/*.conf`) override `Environment=`, and a later `EnvironmentFile=` can too ([[reference_systemd_environmentfile_overrides_environment_2026-07-12]]).
4. Every gate issue must have a paired scheduled check (CLAUDE.md Session-Close §2b). #1594 had none, which is why it drifted 13 days unnoticed.

Both repos affected (`sentiment-agent` AND `predmarket-data`) ⇒ this is the **GitHub App
installation / repo grant for the Claude Code cloud environment**, not a per-routine fault.

CLAUDE.md §2b makes a scheduled check **the deadman for every gate**: *"a gate issue with no
scheduled check is incomplete."* That entire mechanism has been returning nothing since ~2026-06.
The routines did not error loudly — they were **auto-disabled**, so the failure mode is silence,
and every gate opened since then has believed it had a deadman it did not have.

## The replacement pattern — SHIPPED for #1895, reuse it for every gate

User chose the VPS-side timer. `gate-1895-check.timer` on VPS3 (PRs #1994 + #1995),
`OnCalendar=2026-08-13 09:00:00 UTC`, `Persistent=true`. Three properties worth copying:

- **Blanking happens AFTER the summary is read**, so a held arm must still be present in the run
  summary. Otherwise a hold could smuggle a genuinely missing arm past the every-arm-present check.
- **The hold is keyed on PRESENCE, not a date comparison.** A date would make the generator
  time-dependent (the committed `leaderboard.js` would drift from its regeneration and fail CI for
  no reason), and it would expire SILENTLY. Deleting the entry is a deliberate act performed
  exactly when somebody should confirm the window closed rather than merely elapsed.

# Operational Runbooks

> Procedures triggered on-demand (gate fires, promotion, experiment closure). Not daily reference.

## Gate-check Workflow

Triggered when a gate date fires (GitHub Issue with `gate` label).

1. **Read the GitHub issue** (`gh issue view N`) for criteria checklist. Cross-ref the linked memory file for technical detail (N, WR, p-value, alpha).
2. **Query VPS** live DB for current value (via `paper_trades`, `composite_signals`, `calibration_log`, or system-specific table).
3. **Compare** vs gate criteria. Verdict: `PASS` / `FAIL` / `NEEDS_DATA` (N below target).
4. **Propose action**:
   - `PASS` -> run **Shadow->Live Promotion** (below).
   - `FAIL` -> run **Closure Protocol** (below).
   - `NEEDS_DATA` -> comment on issue, extend date in memory, keep

Every DOGE signal was dropped at the executor. Worse, it was

baseline_items.text:
**Refusing known-BAD values is a negative check. It closes only the failure modes you thought of,
and everything the producer never emits — or that predates the field — walks straight through.**

Measured, RE-call `fix/beam-artifact-rejudgeable`, 2026-08-07. I wrote `embed_parity.py` to stop a
GPU-vs-CPU comparison silently running CPU-vs-CPU. Three guards in it could not fire:

🔑 The closed form is `if meta.get("providers_source") != "session": refuse` — require the
known-good value. It rejects nothing the producer emits and everything it does not.

🔑 **A test that hand-crafts an input the producer cannot produce is not a test of the guard.**
That is how #3 shipped green.

inheriting the defect, and that only an audit by other agents caught it.

## Why the usual checks did not catch it
- `git status --short` was **clean** — and clean says nothing about *which commit* you are on.
- The empirical test was real, reproducible, and executed the actual function. Running the code is
  normally the strongest evidence available; here it faithfully measured **the wrong tree**.
- Three sibling clones exist (`~/Documents/RE-call`, `re-call`, `recall`) on different branches.
  Picking one by name and finding a git repo is not picking the right one.

🔑 **Evidence quality does not survive a wrong substrate.** Verifying harder (running vs reading)
made the false finding *more* convincing, not less.

## How to apply — before using code to judge any claim
1. `git rev-parse HEAD` vs `git rev-parse origin/@{u}` (after `git fetch`) — or just
   `git status -sb`, whose `[behind N]` is the part that matters. `--short` alone HIDES it.
2. When several clones of one repo exist, confirm the remote AND the branch AND the distance from
   the tip before reading a line.
3. If a finding contradicts the project's own docs, treat the contradiction as evidence about
   **your inputs** first. These docs are written at implementation time by the person who wrote the
   code; "the doc is wrong AND the test coverage is missing AND it's security-critical" is a
   conjunction rare enough to re-check the substrate before reporting.

## Second instance, same day: sizing a flaky-test fix on the wrong substrate
Fixing RE-call's HNSW corpus fixture (PR #77), I measured the pathology's reproduction rate on the
**local dev pgvector 0.8.4** — 11/14 builds, p≈0.79 — and sized the retry cap at 8. But the suite
that goes red runs on CI's `pgvector/pgvector:pg16` image: its own record showed **2 give-ups in
~76 job-runs at 4 attempts (~2.6e-2), ~13× what the local p predicted**. Correct cap 12, not 8.
🔑 **When a flaky fix is sized from a rate, the rate must come from the environment that fails.**
A local reproduction proves the mechanism; it does not measure the frequency. Prefer the CI failure
record (scan recent runs for the failure string) over any number you can produce on your own box.

**The right test for "does this branch still add anything?" is `git merge -X ours` followed by `git diff --cached` against master.** Not `merge-tree` on its own.

**Why:** with conflicts present, the merge tree ALWAYS differs from master, so "it adds something" is vacuous — the answer is yes by construction. Resolving conflicts in master's favour and then measuring the residue is the only form of the test that can come back **"nothing"**. Applied to 11 RE-call branches on 2026-07-28, **5 came back with zero residue**.

**How to apply:**

- ⚠️ "Is this string already on master?" does NOT prove supersession either. It confirms that *almost* everything landed and that you have not yet found the residue.
- 🔑 For a **squash-merged** branch, `git log master..branch` lies — every commit looks unmerged.
- 🔑 The `ddd` ruleset was removed by the user, so `git push --delete` works.
- Record the SHAs before deleting: a deleted branch tip stays recoverable while the reflog holds it.

Related: [[feedback-concurrent-sessions-race-the-same-clone-2026-07-24]] — `git merge-tree` CLEAN does not mean no collision either.

- `git status --short` was **clean** — and clean says nothing about *which commit* you are on.
- The empirical test was real, reproducible, and executed the actual function. Running the code is
  normally the strongest evidence available; here it faithfully measured **the wrong tree**.

🔑 **Evidence quality does not survive a wrong substrate.** Verifying harder (running vs reading)
made the false finding *more* convincing, not less.

   the tip before reading a line.

   **your inputs** first. These docs are written at implementation time by the person who wrote the
   code; "the doc is wrong AND the test coverage is missing AND it's security-critical" is a
   conjunction rare enough to re-check the substrate before reporting.

Without one, sudo for any non-allowlisted command silently fails with "a terminal is required to read the password" — the operator is locked out of every ad-hoc admin operation, and even console root login becomes the only recovery path.

**How to apply:**

- Even when a password exists, double-check the operator can recover via console — every Cmnd_Alias deploy needs a documented break-glass path that's been tested.
- Keep the pre-deploy file backup at a path the new sudoers still permits to read (so post-deploy rollback to the prior policy is possible from the same shell). The 2026-05-05 deploy left the backup at `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment.bak.<TS>` — DENIED to read by the new

The password actually *was* set, but the user couldn't remember it — equivalent to no fallback. - Even when a password exists, double-check the operator can recover via console — every Cmnd_Alias deploy needs a documented break-glass path that's been tested.

User `sentiment` è in sudo group (`(ALL : ALL) ALL` con password) MA ha un set NOPASSWD specifico. Sapere cosa è coperto evita di proporre comandi che falliscono o richiedono interazione interattiva.

## NOPASSWD coperti (eseguibili autonomamente da Claude via ssh)

**Systemd**: `systemctl restart|start|stop|reload|status|cat|is-active|is-enabled|is-failed|reset-failed|enable|disable|show *`, `systemctl list-units|list-timers|list-unit-files [*]`.

**Journalctl**: `journalctl *` (incluso `--vacuum-time`, `--vacuum-size`, `--disk-usage`).

**File ops in /opt/sentiment_agent**: `chmod NNN[N] [-R]`, `chown [-R] sentiment:sentiment`, `rm -rf /opt/sentiment_agent/__pycache__` e `*/__pycache__`.

- Pulizia disco low-risk (`pip cache purge`, `rm __pycache__`, `journalctl --vacuum-*`, `rm` in /opt) → autonomo OK
- Install nuovi tool (glances, lnav, tuned, earlyoom, qualsiasi `apt install`) → richiede l'utente
- Config kernel/perf (`sysctl`, `tuned-adm`, `logrotate.d` write) → richiede l'utente
- Restart/reload systemd unit + cat unit file + journal tail → autonomo OK
- PG queries via `sudo -u postgres psql -d sentiment_agent` → autonomo OK
- Modifiche a `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment` per estendere allowlist: **destructive, mai senza conferma esplicita** (cf. `feedback_check_password_before_sudo_lockdown.md`).

## NON coperti (richiedono password sudo, NON eseguire autonomamente)

- `apt`, `apt-get`, `apt install|update|upgrade|autoremove|clean` — install/cleanup pacchetti
- `tee` verso path arbitrari (es. `/etc/sysctl.d/`, `/etc/logrotate.d/`) — solo `/etc/sentiment/healthcheck.url` è coperto
- `sysctl --system`, `sysctl -w` — tweak kernel
- `tuned-adm profile *` — performance tuning
- `logrotate` (esecuzione + config write)
- `usermod`, `gpasswd`, `passwd root` — esplicitamente `!` (negate, mai concessi)
- `visudo` — esplicitamente `!` negate
- `cat /root/age/*` e variants — esplicitamente `!` (age key protection)
- `docker` per container fuori dal set monitoring (no general `docker exec`, `docker run`, `docker build`)

query.query: why can gate 1774 never turn green

items.text:
⇒ **3 fills is a conservative LOWER BOUND** against a measured 87k–4.8M share queue at the touch —
it is a statement about our simulator's blindness to cancels, **not** a market fact that resting at
the touch does not fill. Real books drain by cancellation too. The hypothesis is **still untested**.

## Why it was not re-dated

This is the **2nd phantom-gate diagnosis on this same gate** (the 1st was 07-19, comment
`5015109734`). Both times the collector was alive and the gate still could not reach its bar.
Extending the date a third time without building (a) cancel attribution and (b) the markout writer
just re-runs the phantom. **A gate that cannot turn green only speaks about itself.**

1. **`ended` is never true.** `under_decay_game_state` holds 71,381 frames over 841 games and
   **not one has `ended=true`**; `period` only ever takes `1H`/`2H` and frames simply stop at
   elapsed 90. `runner.on_state()` gates settlement on `if state.ended:` and nothing else calls
   `settle_position()`, so `under_decay_positions.status` has never left `'open'` and
   `realized_usd` has never been written. `report.gate_report()` filters
   `status='settled' AND realized_usd IS NOT NULL` ⇒ `n_settled=0`, `has_data=false` **by
   construction, permanently**. Criteria 2 (calibration, the PRIMARY one) and 3 (net EV) are
   therefore *unmeasurable*, not merely unmet.

**2026-08-27, three times.** Every time CI went red on something a local run would have caught. The
first two were gates run *before* the change; the third was a gate my own filter never selected.

1. **mypy on PR #532.** I ran ruff and pytest after editing `sdk_exec.py` and did not re-run mypy,
   which had been green earlier. The new parameter was `StdioRecallSpec | None` where the callee
   wanted `StdioRecallSpec`.
2. **The citation gates after merging `recall_agent`.** My insertion in `recall/store.py` shifted
   every line below it by 26, invalidating four `path:line` citations in the docs. The gates had
   been green before the insertion.

🔑 This is the **phantom-gate class** again ([[feedback-verify-collector-terminal-table-2026-07-14]]):
the service is `active`, `game_state` ingests today, `markets` refresh today — every liveness signal
is green while the terminal table has never once been written. Same shape as #1932 and #1761.
🔑 **Extending the date accrues nothing** until the fix lands: fix terminal-frame detection,
reconcile the 3 zombies, backfill, *then* re-date.

**Why this keeps happening:** a green gate produces a feeling of coverage that outlives the state
it described, and nothing in the terminal distinguishes "green, and nothing has changed since" from
"green, four edits ago". It is exactly the staleness failure this project documents everywhere
else, applied to my own working memory instead of to a note.

**How to apply:**

- **The last thing before staging is the full gate set, in one command, from this worktree's root.**
  Not the subset that seems related: the mypy failure was in a file whose change looked purely
  additive, and the citation failure was in documents I never opened.

**How to apply:**
- Session-Close §2c (gate resolved → comment + close) is incomplete: also **cancel or repoint
  the paired scheduled check** in the same session.
- When a scheduled gate task fires, **read the issue state FIRST**. `state: CLOSED` ⇒ the correct
  output is a SUPERSEDED note on the issue, not a run.
- Do not treat "the run is technically feasible" as a reason to run. #1494's substrate was still
  writing and the tuner still imported cleanly; the blocker was economic (`rewardsMinSize`
  20→200 priced us out), and no allocator result could move it.
  See [[project-lrp-reward-farming-closed-venue-repricing-2026-07-16]] and
  [[feedback-venue-can-reprice-you-out-overnight-2026-07-16]].

1. Partial ingest faking a FAIL (v1 ladder) · 2. absent data faking a FAIL (`paired_difference_ci`
returning `(0,0,0)`) · 3. **empty corpus faking a PASS** (`d=max` ingested zero documents; v1's H1
PASS was an artefact) · 4. a vacuous test that stayed green with **every label flipped** ·
5. an invariant advertised in the spec and **never called** · 6. an empty denominator rendering as
`0.0` — an ABSENCE printed as a measured perfect result · 7. `importorskip` on an extra `.[dev]`
never installs, in a **merge-gating job** ⇒ green and useless exactly where it decides ·
8. **the inversion** (mem-bench, 07-30): `independently-reproduced` could not fire *at all*, because
`below_floor` was an integer count compared against a 0.005 **float** tolerance — one row out of
1200 differing denied the

2. **The 3 zombie positions saturate the concurrency cap.** `count_open_positions()` counts
   `status='open'` and `max_concurrent_matches=3`. The last BUY (2026-07-26 11:37:43) is exactly the
   entry that filled slot 3; in the 20 days since there were 1,052 in-window signals and **zero**
   BUYs, 29 of them rejected explicitly as `concurrency cap` (08-11, elapsed 52-80′, avg ret +0.28 —
   entries the strategy wanted). `fits_by_key` is a plain in-memory dict wiped by the 2026-07-31
   06:06 restart, so those 3 can never self-clear even if `ended` were fixed. **n is frozen at 4/30.**

**How to apply:**
1. When a CI job is red, ask *"has this EVER been green?"* before assuming the current failure is the
   whole story. A job with no green in its history is broken as a gate, not failing as a check.
2. Fixing one cause does not validate the fix — **re-run and look again.** Each of the four above was
   only visible after the previous merge.
3. To test "X is not present", grep for X across the whole artifact. Never conclude absence from a
   `head -40`.
4. When a comparison drives a gate, check what the compared artifact rewrites on every run
   (timestamps, ordering, generated fields). Compare the SEMANTIC content, not bytes — and verify the
   loosened comparison still catches a real change (I injected a synthetic finding to prove the
   timestamp filter had not blinded

🔑 **A gate that cannot go green reports nothing about the tree — it only reports itself.** Same
family as the phantom-gate class and "`is-active` is not evidence a service works": #3 and #4 each
made the job *look* like it was checking something. Nobody had ever seen it pass, which should have
been the tell far earlier than it was.

## The verification mistake worth not repeating

**Why:** this is a specific instance of the standing rule that **a gate that cannot go green tells
you only about itself**. A gate failing on infrastructure drift is worse than one failing on a
finding, because the red is attributed to the plumbing and the missing coverage is never noticed.
It also rhymes with **CI GREEN ≠ CHECKED** — here it was CI RED ≠ CHECKED, same blind spot.

Closing a `gate` issue early (lane death, venue repricing, moot verdict) leaves its paired
`/schedule` deadman armed. On 2026-07-21 the `maker-net-tuner-gate-run` task fired for gate
#1494 — closed 2026-07-16 with the LRP lane. The task instructions still read as a live gate
("ahead of the 2026-07-21 gate") and prescribed training + posting a learned-vs-baseline
verdict.

— I called an archive missing after searching three drives; it was at `f83a330^`, and my filename filter could never have matched it.
- [External state in generated assets](external-state-in-generated-assets.md) — fetch it so a rebuild shows drift (caught Glama AAA→AAB); prose has no rebuild, and sample before believing one fetch.
- [Fixes leak outside the file you edited](fixes-leak-outside-the-file-you-edited.md) — 20 of 22 review findings were in my own fixes; test the artifact a reader opens, not the return value.
- [Green PR checks can predate a new CI job](green-pr-checks-can-predate-a-new-ci-job.md) — 8/8 SUCCESS and CLEAN described the jobs that existed at last build; a job master added afterwards never ran, and two green PRs turned master red on merge. **Compare check COUNTS, not

**Why:** CLAUDE.md §2b makes every gate carry a scheduled check as its deadman, but there is no
inverse rule. An orphaned deadman is worse than a missing one: it arrives with confident,
self-contained instructions and no knowledge that the lane died, so the default behaviour is to
re-run a closed experiment and post numbers that invite a reopen. The scheduled task's own
framing is stale data, not authority — [[feedback-verify-collector-terminal-table-2026-07-14]]
is the same failure shape one layer down.

🔑 **The part worth keeping: 18 of the 24 were wrong and GREEN.** The anchor checker only fails when
the cited line's anchor falls outside its window, and a shift of a few lines stays inside it. So a
passing citation gate is evidence that a pointer is close, not that it is right, which is the same
shape as the note in `CLAUDE.md` about a green `git merge` not proving a server still serves.

Two rules this leaves standing: `docs/preregistrations/` and `docs/archive/` are frozen and were not
touched (the standing instruction forbids editing a number in a committed pre-registration, and a
gate must never force that edit), and a citation is better written against a SYMBOL than a line
where a symbol will do.
